Suretiship
SHOOR-ti-ship
n. (the standing of a surety; the assuming of another's debt)
Hebrew taqa, to strike, as in striking hands to seal a pledge — the gesture that bound a man to another's debt. Latin securitas, through Old French surte: the condition of one who stands security for another.

Biblical Definition

He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure. A surety is a man who makes himself liable for another's debt, and the wisdom literature returns to the practice repeatedly with the same counsel: do not do it. Proverbs is not condemning generosity — it commands giving throughout — but a specific arrangement in which a man pledges his own solvency against an obligation he does not control. The warnings are urgent and practical: be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts; if thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? And, a man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend. The reason is plain enough. The surety carries all the risk and none of the decisions, and the man who has accepted such a position may find his household ruined by another man's choices. There is a striking exception, and Scripture builds its greatest doctrine on it. Hebrews says of Christ, By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament. He did exactly what Proverbs warns a man not to do — assumed liability for debtors who could not pay, with full knowledge of the cost — and the thing Proverbs says will make a man smart is precisely what happened at the cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another and make good any debt or loss which may arise from another's delinquency.

expand to see more

SURETISHIP, n. The state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another, and to make good any debt or loss which may occur from another's delinquency.

SURETY, n. One that is bound with and for another; one who enters into a bond or recognizance to answer for another's appearance, or for his payment of a debt.

SURETY, n. Security; safety; certainty; indubitableness.

BOND, n. An obligation or deed by which a person binds himself, his heirs, executors and administrators, to pay a certain sum on or before a future day appointed.

SMART, v.i. To feel a lively pungent pain; to bear a penalty or the evil consequences of any thing.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 11:15 — "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure."

Proverbs 22:26 — "Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts."

Proverbs 17:18 — "A man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend."

Hebrews 7:22 — "By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs' counsel is read either as a general endorsement of financial self-protection or dismissed as ancient advice; and the doctrine it prepares — Christ as surety — is weakened wherever the atonement is made less than substitutionary.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the turning of prudential wisdom into a principle of self-protection that overrides plain commands. Proverbs warns against assuming liability for debts a man cannot control; it nowhere teaches him to keep his money safe from his brother's need. The same book commands giving to the poor, and the New Testament commands bearing one another's burdens. Wisdom literature gives counsel for the ordinary case, and a Christian who cites Proverbs 11:15 to avoid sacrificial generosity has quoted the right verse for the wrong purpose.

The doctrinal weight of the word lies in Hebrews 7:22, and it is lost wherever the atonement is made something less than substitution. If the cross is chiefly a demonstration of love, or an example of self-giving, or a victory over powers with no debt actually transferred, then surety is a metaphor with nothing behind it. Scripture means it legally. Christ stood in the place of debtors, assumed an obligation that was not his, and discharged it in his own body — which is why Proverbs' warning is so illuminating by contrast. What is folly for a man void of understanding was, for the Son of God, deliberate, costly, and undertaken with full knowledge of the price.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew taqa (H8628), to strike, as hands in pledge; arab (H6148), to become surety; zur (H2114), a stranger; Greek egguos (G1450), a surety.

expand to see more

Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to strike, as striking hands to seal a pledge; behind suretiship.

Hebrew arab (H6148) — to give in pledge, to become surety for another.

Hebrew zur (H2114) — a stranger; the one for whom suretiship is most dangerous.

Hebrew raa (H7489) — to be broken, to suffer hurt; rendered shall smart for it.

Greek egguos (G1450) — a surety, one who gives security; used of Jesus at Hebrews 7:22, its only occurrence.

Usage

"“he that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it” — the prudential warning."

"“be not thou one of them that strike hands” — the gesture that bound a man."

"“Jesus made a surety of a better testament” — the one who did it knowingly."
